title: When Rewards Backfire
objective: After this level you can explain intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and how rewards can undermine interest.
summary: Doing something for its own sake is intrinsic motivation. An expected, tangible reward can shrink it, as preschoolers with magic markers showed in 1973.

cards.headline: Reward a child for drawing, and they may draw less.
cards.body: In 1973, at Stanford's Bing Nursery School, psychologists offered preschoolers who already loved drawing with magic markers a shiny Good Player Award. Weeks later, the children promised the award had cooled on drawing. How can a prize make a favorite activity less fun?

cards.headline: Two kinds of reason
cards.body: Psychologists split motivation into two kinds. Intrinsic motivation means you do something for the satisfaction it brings, like doodling because doodling is fun. Extrinsic motivation means you do it to get something from others: a grade, a paycheck, a gold star. Most of what you do mixes both. The trouble starts when one kind crowds out the other.

cards.headline: The Good Player Award
cards.body: Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett split the young artists into groups. Some were promised the award for drawing; some got it as a surprise afterward; some got nothing. One to two weeks later, observers watched free play. Children who had drawn for the expected award spent about 8.6 percent of their free time drawing, about half as much as the other two groups.

cards.headline: When rewards backfire
cards.body: This is the overjustification effect: an outside reward can shrink the inside reason, until effort depends on the reward. It isn't a one-off. A 1999 meta-analysis of 128 studies found expected and tangible rewards undermined intrinsic motivation, while positive feedback boosted it. Money tends to hurt more than praise, and a surprise reward tends to leave interest intact.

questions.prompt: In Lepper's 1973 marker study, which preschoolers later spent the least free time drawing?

options.label: Those given a surprise award after drawing
options.rationale: Surprise-award children kept drawing about as much as before.

options.label: Those who never received any award
options.rationale: The no-award group drew about as much as the surprise group.

options.label: Those promised the Good Player Award
Those who had never used markers before
options.rationale: All the children already liked drawing with markers.

questions.explanation: Children who drew for an expected award later spent about 8.6 percent of free time drawing, about half as much as the other groups.

questions.prompt: Why did a surprise award leave children's interest intact when an expected award did not?

options.label: Surprise awards were bigger and shinier
options.rationale: Both groups got the same award.

options.label: Interest tends to persist when a reward is not expected
The surprise group never saw the markers again
options.rationale: All groups had markers during free play.

options.label: Praise was banned for the expected group
options.rationale: The study compared expectation, not praise.

questions.explanation: When a reward is expected, the activity starts to feel like a means to it; a surprise reward tends to leave intrinsic motivation intact.

questions.prompt: Level 41's incentives pull behavior from outside. Why can adding one to an activity you already love backfire?

options.label: Incentives only work on animals in a Skinner box
options.rationale: Incentives work on people too; paychecks are incentives.

options.label: It makes the activity physically harder to do
Incentives always cancel out every drive
options.rationale: Drives and incentives usually work together.

options.label: The outside reason can crowd out the inside one

questions.explanation: That is the overjustification effect: an expected outside reward can shrink intrinsic motivation, so effort comes to depend on the reward.
